               <ns0:p n="5">5 Even so the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Prov. 12.18. and 15.2.</ns0:note> tongue is a little member <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">The Accomodation of the former Similitudes: the Tongue is a little Member, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> one of the lesser, in Comparison of the Body.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Psal. 12.3. and 73.8, 9.</ns0:note> boasteth great things <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> Word signifies, according to its Derivation, the lifting up of the Neck (as Horses, mentioned, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 3. are wont to do in their Pride) in a way of Bravery and Triumph; and hence it is used to express boasting and glorying, but here seems to imply something more, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> not only the uttering big Words, but doing great things, whether good and useful, as in the former Similitudes, or evil, as in what follows; or its boasting how great things it can do, <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> the Tongue, tho little, is of great force and efficacy, and it will tell you so it self; it not only boasts what its fellow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />Members can do, but especially what it self can.</ns0:note>. Behold how great <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Another Similitude in which he sets forth the evil the Tongue, as lit<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tle as it is, doth, where it is not well-governed, as in the for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mer he had shewn the good it may do, when kept under Rule.</ns0:note> a <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>wood.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> matter <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">The word signifies either any comoustible Stuff, or, as in the Margin, <ns0:hi>Wood,</ns0:hi> that being the ordinary Fuel then in use.</ns0:note> a little fire kindleth <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Even a Spark, the smallest Quantity or Particle, which may do great Mischief, when lighting in sutable matter.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 And the tongue <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> a fire <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">The Application of the Similitude in the foregoing Words. The Tongue is a Fire, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> hath the force of Fire, and resembles it in the Mischief it doth.</ns0:note>, a world <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">A<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> Heap, or Ag<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gregation of Evils (as the natural World is an Aggregation of many several Beings) as we say, an Ocean, or a World of Troubles, meaning, a great Multitude of them. And the Words may be understood, either with an <ns0:hi>Ellipsis</ns0:hi> of the word <ns0:hi>matter,</ns0:hi> expressed just before, and supplied here; and the pointing a little altered, they may be thus read, <ns0:hi>And the Tongue is a Fire, a World of Iniquity</ns0:hi> (or an unrighteous World, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> which lies in Wickedness, 1 <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 5.19.) is the <ns0:hi>matter,</ns0:hi> namely, which it inflames. A wicked World is fit Fuel for a wicked Tongue, and soon catcheth the Fire which it kindles: Or, rather as they stand plainly without any such Defect: The Tongue is a World of Iniquity, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> an Heap or Mass of various sorts of Sins; tho it be but a little piece of Flesh, yet it contains a whole Word of Wickedness in it, or is as full of Evils, as the World is of Bodies.</ns0:note> of ini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quity: So is the tongue amongst our members, that <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 15.11, 18, 19. Mark. 7.15, 20, 23.</ns0:note> it defileth the whole body <ns0:hi>q,</ns0:hi> and setteth on fire the course of nature <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Or, setteth on Fire <ns0:hi>the Wheel of Geniture, or Nativity</ns0:hi> (in allusion to a Wheel set on fire by a violent rapid motion) meaning the Course of Nativity, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> the natural Course of Life, as the Face of Nativity or Geniture, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 1.23. for the natural Face; the sense is, it inflames with various Lusts, Wrath, Malice, Wantonness, Pride, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> the whole Course of Man's Life, so that there is no State, nor Age free from the Evils of it. Whereas other Vices either do not extend to the whole Man, or are abated with Age, or worn away with length of time; the Vices of the Tongue reach the whole Man, and the whole time of his life.</ns0:note>; and it is set on fire of hell.<ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">i. e. By the Devil, the Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther of Lyes and Slanders, and other Tongue-sins, <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 1.10. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 8.44. <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 12.10. the Tongue being the Fire, the Devil, by the Bellows of Temptations, inflames it yet more, and thereby kindles the Fire of all Mischiefs in the World.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Infecteth the whole Man with Sin, <ns0:hi>Eccles.</ns0:hi> 5.6. as being the cause of Sin committed by all the Members of the Body; for tho Sin be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gin in the Soul, yet it is executed by the Body, which there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore seems here put (as <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 2.) for the <ns0:hi>Man.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>

                  </ns0:note> kind <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Some of every kind.</ns0:note> of beasts <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Wild Beasts, such as are most fierce and untractable.</ns0:note>, and of birds <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Tho so moveable and wandring, the very Vagabonds of Nature,</ns0:note>, and of serpents <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">which are such Enemies to Mankind.</ns0:note>, and things in the sea <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">The Inhabitants, as it were, of another World; really of another Element.</ns0:note>, is tamed, and hath been tamed <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Either made gentle, or at least, brought into Subjection to Man by one means or other He useth both Tenses, the Present, and the Preterperfect, to note that such things, not only have been, but still are; and that not as the Effects of some miraculous Providence, as in the Case of <ns0:hi>Daniel,</ns0:hi> ch. 6, and <ns0:hi>Paul,</ns0:hi> Acts· 28. but as that which is u<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sually experienced, and in Man's Power still to do.</ns0:note> of <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Gr. <ns0:hi>Nature of</ns0:hi>

               <ns0:p n="8">8 <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Not only other Men's Tongues, but not his own.</ns0:note> But the tongue can no man tame <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">No Man of himself, and without the Assistance of Di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vine Grace, can bring his Tongue into Subjection, and keep it in order; nor can any. Man by the Assistance of any Grace promised in this Life, so keep it, as that it shall never at all offend.</ns0:note>: <ns0:hi>it is</ns0:hi> an unruly evil <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Or, which cannot be restrained, and kept within Bounds: Wild Beasts are kept in by Grates and Bars, but this by no Restraint.</ns0:note>, full of deadly poison <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">The Wickedness of the Tongue is compared to Poison<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> in respect of the Mischief it doth to others. It seems to allude to those kind of Serpents which have Poison under their Tongues, <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> 140.3. with which they kill those they bite. The Poison of the Tongue is no less deadly, it murders Men's Reputations by the Slanders it utters, their Souls by the Lust, and <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>assions it stirs up in them, and many times their Bodies too by the Contentions and Quarrels it raiseth against Men.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 Therewith bless we God <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Prays, and speak well of God.</ns0:note> even the Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Of Christ, and in him of all true Believers.</ns0:note>, and therewith curse we men <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Rail on, revile, speak evil of, as well as wish evil to.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>en. 1.26.</ns0:note> which are made after the similitude of God <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Either, 1. Saints in whom God's Image is anew restored; or, 2ly. rather Men more generally, who, tho they have lost that spiritual Knowledge, Righte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ousness, and true Holiness, in which that Image of God, af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter which Man was created, principally consists; yet still have some Reliques of his Image continuing in them. This is ad<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ded to aggravate the Sin, speaking evil of Men made after God's Image, is speaking evil of God obliquely, and by Reflection.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 Out of the same mouth proceedeth bles<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sing and cursing <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">He repeats here, by way of Exaggeration, what he had said, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 9. to shew how exceedingly absurd it is, that two such contrary Actions should proceed from the same Agent.</ns0:note>. My brethren, these things ought not so to be <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">There is a <ns0:hi>M<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>iosis</ns0:hi> in the words; he means, things should be quite contrary. See the like Expression, 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 5.13. <ns0:hi>Tit.</ns0:hi> 1.11.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 Doth a fountain send forth at the same <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>hole.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> place <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Ordinarily and naturally; if any such be, it is looked upon as uncouth and prodigious.</ns0:note> sweet <ns0:hi>water</ns0:hi> and bitter?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 Can the fig-tree, my brethren, bear olive berries, either a vine figs <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">The same Tree cannot ordinarily bring forth Fruit of dif<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ferent kinds (on the same Branch, whatever it may on different, by engrafting) much less contrary Natures. See <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 7.16, 17, 18.</ns0:note>? So <ns0:hi>can</ns0:hi> no fountain yield both salt water, and fresh <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>neither can a salt Fountain yield fresh Water</ns0:hi>; but the Scope is still the same, as in our reading. The Apostle argues from what is impossible, or monstrous in Naturals, to what is absurd in Manners, <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> it is as absurd in Religion, for the Tongue of a regenerate Man, which is used to bless God, to take a liberty at other times to curse Man, as it would be strange in Nature for the same Tree, on the same Branch, to bear Fruits of different kinds; or the same Fountain at the same place to send forth bitter Water and sweet.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 Who <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e. If there be a wise Man,</ns0:hi> &c. See <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> 25.12. and 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 3.10. where what <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> speaks by way of Interrogation, <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> explains by way of Assertion. The Apostle having shewn the Disease of the Tongue, comes now to remove the Cause, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> Mens Opinion of their own Wisdom; (they censure others, because they take themselves to be wiser than others) and to point out the Remedy, godly Meek<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness, which is the truest Wisdom.</ns0:note> a wise man, and endued with knowledge <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">By Wisdom and Know<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledge the same thing may be meant; or if they be taken for several things, (as sometimes there may be great Know<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledge where there is but little Wisdom) yet these master<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly Censors he speaks of, pretended to both, and were so rigid toward others, because so well conceited of themselves: the sense is, You pretend to be wise and knowing, but if you would approve your selves as such indeed, <ns0:hi>shew out of a good Conversation,</ns0:hi> &c.</ns0:note> among you? let him shew, out of a good conversation, his works <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Let him shew as the Testimony of his Wisdom, not his words in hard Censures, but his Works, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> good ones, and those not done now and then, or on the by, but in the constant Course, and Tenor of his Life<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> or shew his Works to be good, by their being not casual, but constant, and his ordinary Practice in his whole Conversation.</ns0:note> with meekness of wisdom <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Meek and gentle Wisdom, which can hear, and answer, and teach, and admonish, and rebuke mildly, and sweetly, with long-suffering, as well as Doctrine, 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 4.2. and then it notes the Quality of this Wisdom, or such Meekness as proceeds from Wisdom, or is joyn<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed with it, there being some which is foolish, affected, car<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nal, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> that which is opposed to Zeal; whereas true Meek<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness is only opposed to Fierceness and Rashness; and thus it notes the cause of Meekness.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 But if ye have <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 13.13.</ns0:note> bitter envying <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Gr. <ns0:hi>Zeal,</ns0:hi> which he calls bitter, partly to distinguish it from that Zeal which is good; whereas this he speaks of is evil; and though it pretends to be Zeal, yet is really no other than Envy; and partly because it commonly proceeds from an imbittered Spirit, and tends to the imbittering it more.</ns0:note>, and strife <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Strife, the usual Effect of bitter Zeal, or Envy.</ns0:note> in your hearts <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">The Fountain whence it proceeds; or Strife in the Heart implies a Heart propense, and inclined to Strife.</ns0:note>, glory not <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Glory not of your Zeal, or rather, of your Wisdom, as if you were so well able to reprehend others, but rather be hum<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bled; what you make the matter of your glorying, being really just cause of Shame.</ns0:note>, and lie not against the truth <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> By professing your selves wife, or zealous, when ye are really neither.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 This wisdom <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">This Wisdom which they pretended so much to, who so criticized on other Men's Actions, and inveighed against them, and which was accompanied with Strife and Envy.</ns0:note> descendeth not from a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bove <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> From God the Author of Wisdom, from whom, tho every good and perfect Gift descends, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 1.17. and even Knowledge, and Skill in natural things, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 28.26<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 29, yet this Wisdom being sinful, is not from him,</ns0:note>, but <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> earthly <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">because it is of the Earth, of no higher Original than from the first <ns0:hi>Adam,</ns0:hi> who was of the Earth, and earthly, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 15.47. and like<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wise because it is employed, and fixeth Mens Minds on earthly things.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>natural.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> sensual <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">This may be understood, either, 1. accord<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing to the reading in the Text, the word here used, being so rendred, <ns0:hi>Iude</ns0:hi> 1.9. agreeable to 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 5.23. where <ns0:hi>Soul,</ns0:hi> from whence the word is derived, is opposed to <ns0:hi>Spirit,</ns0:hi> and taken for the sensitive Powers, which Men have in common with Brutes in Distinction from the intellectual, which go under the name of Spirit, and are proper to Men: meer Reason, without the Divine Grace, being apt to degenerate into Brutishness, and easily brought to serve the ends of sensual Appetite; this VVisdom may well be called sensual. Or, 2ly. according to the margin, <ns0:hi>Natural,</ns0:hi> in opposition to <ns0:hi>Spiritual.</ns0:hi> The natural Man (1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 2.14. where the same word (in the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi>) is used as here) is one that lives un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der the Conduct of his own carnal Reason, not enlightned, nor regenerated by the Spirit of God: <ns0:hi>A Man of Soul,</ns0:hi> (as the word imports) or that hath no better, no higher Principle in him, than his own Soul. Accordingly, this VVisdom here mentioned, is such as proceeds meerly from a Man's own Soul, in its natural state destitute of the Light and Grace of God's Spirit, and therefore may be termed <ns0:hi>natural.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, devilish <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Because it is of the Devil, or such as is in him, and makes Men like him, who is a proud Spirit, and envious, a Lier, and Slanderer, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 8.44. and who observes Mens Faults, not to amend them, but accuse them for them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
